About the estimates

Model scope & limitations

Retirement Forecast - Monte Carlo Simulator is an educational scenario planner. It is designed for U.S. retirement planning only. Its results are hypothetical estimates, not predictions or guarantees of what will happen to you.

How the Monte Carlo simulation works

The planner runs many possible retirement lifetimes from the same starting assumptions. In each path it samples market returns, general inflation, healthcare inflation, and lifespan, then calculates monthly income, spending, taxes, and withdrawals. The free preview runs four paths. Pro subscribers can select up to 10,000 paths under Assumptions → Market & withdrawal strategy → Advanced model settings or Plans & billing. Both versions use the same fixed random sequence, and all calculations run in your browser.

The charts show the spread of those modeled outcomes rather than a single straight-line forecast. Four paths are too small a sample to estimate retirement readiness. Preview results show counts such as “4 of 4” instead of a readiness percentage; even 4 of 4 without a shortfall does not imply certain success. More paths can make the estimate steadier, but they cannot make incorrect assumptions accurate or capture every future event.

What “readiness” means

The readiness percentage is the share of simulated lifetimes that did not run out of portfolio funds under the inputs and assumptions selected. It is not the probability that your actual plan will succeed. A different set of assumptions, simulation count, or future events can change the result. The model cannot represent every possible outcome.

Reported medians average the two middle observations when the sample count is even. Funding and survival curves include monthly shortfalls and deaths through the last modeled lifetime. A path that ends without a shortfall remains counted as funded; the final funded share equals the run’s readiness. Lifetimes are sampled independently of the maximum modeling age. Paths still alive at that observation limit remain counted as alive; the limit does not force death, move care earlier, or trigger a home sale. Ending balances include the final observed balance at death, the limit, or shortfall.

U.S. scope and laws

The calculator uses simplified U.S. federal ordinary-income tax, Social Security, Medicare, and retirement withdrawal rules. Its tax tables start with 2026 federal brackets and deductions; estimates for later years inflate those figures rather than predicting future laws. It does not calculate state or local income taxes, a complete individual tax return, or laws and benefit systems outside the United States. It should not be used for retirement planning under another country's laws.

Tax and benefit rules can change. Check current rules and your own eligibility with the IRS, Social Security Administration, and Medicare.

Other important assumptions

  • Investment returns and both inflation rates use independent monthly lognormal growth factors calibrated so the compounded twelve-month change has the arithmetic average and standard deviation entered in the assumptions. Negative returns, deflation, and healthcare cost decreases are allowed; monthly factors stay positive without clipping inflation draws. Stocks and bonds are independent and use the same draws across account types. This distribution does not represent every market tail, correlation, or future event.
  • Your birthday, retirement day, and spouse birthday use calendar dates. Dates determine ages, birth-year benefit cohorts, and the first retirement year. Retirement begins today or later. The model uses completed calendar months for age and pre-retirement growth, without daily cash-flow proration; month-end and leap-day anniversaries use the last valid day of the month. Older age-only plans receive estimated dates and a reminder to review them. Pension start age and long-term-care duration accept whole years and extra months from 0 through 11. The model applies these timings by month. Mortality preserves the annual age-specific death probabilities and samples deaths at month ends throughout the year, assuming a constant mortality hazard between birthdays. A partial first year uses only the months before the next birthday. Cash flows, survivor changes, and care timing follow the sampled death month; annual chart observations start at the selected retirement age. Ending balances include any final partial year. Failure ages and their zero-balance endpoints use the actual modeled month rather than the previous retirement anniversary. Planning targets search whole-year retirement ages from the next birthday (or today on a birthday) through 70, or through the last age the maximum modeling age allows. They give the same answer whether the browser checks candidates one at a time or several at once.
  • Before retirement, the model grows the balances you enter using the assumed returns. It does not add future savings contributions or calculate employment income, pre-retirement taxes, or pre-retirement required distributions. Cash earns a fixed 2% annual yield; during retirement, credited interest is ordinary income for federal tax, Social Security taxation, and Medicare income calculations. Withdrawing cash principal does not create income.
  • Taxable brokerage balances receive investment returns, but the model does not calculate capital-gains or dividend taxes or tax on brokerage withdrawals. This can overstate after-tax funds available from those accounts.
  • Ordinary spending withdrawals use pretax savings first, then Roth savings, then taxable brokerage savings, and finally cash. The optional drawdown strategy uses cash first during qualifying market declines. Roth-conversion taxes use cash, taxable savings, Roth savings, then pretax savings. Roth inputs separate total value and remaining regular contributions; past conversions record their tax year, remaining principal, and remaining taxable principal. Contributions are withdrawn first, then conversion years oldest first (taxable principal before nontaxable principal within each year), then earnings. Returns never increase dollar basis, and losses do not reduce it. Nonqualified earnings are ordinary income for federal tax, taxable Social Security, senior deduction phaseouts, conversion limits, and Medicare. With early penalties enabled, earnings and taxable converted principal within its separate five-tax-year period incur 10% before 59½, including converted funds used to pay conversion tax. Conversion principal is not taxed as income again when withdrawn. Earnings generally qualify after the first-funding five-tax-year period and age 59½; inherited distributions in the modeled death year can qualify after the account period without the age requirement. A previously unfunded Roth starts its account clock at the first modeled conversion. Year numbering follows modeled tax years. These are Roth IRA rules; employer Roth 401(k) distributions can differ. The pooled Roth follows the primary-owned and surviving-spouse-own-account assumption used for pretax savings; separate spouse histories and specialized penalty exceptions are excluded. See IRS Publication 590-B.
  • Older saved plans and Android imports did not include Roth history. Their balances are preserved; migration assumes the opening value is remaining regular contributions, first funding in 2021, and no past conversions. The editor, planning notes, and reports mark these assumptions for review. Enter the actual remaining contributions, first funding year, and conversion principal; contribution basis can exceed the current balance after losses.
  • Rule of 55 eligibility is an explicit declaration that the primary-owned pretax pool qualifies for the employer-plan separation exception. Separation during the calendar year the person turns 55 can qualify before their birthday. Because separation must fall in or after that calendar year, the declaration has no effect for a retirement age below 54. It does not exempt IRA distributions or Roth conversion recapture. See IRS early-distribution exceptions.
  • Required minimum distributions use the IRS Uniform Lifetime Table, beginning at age 73 for birth years 1951–1959 or age 75 for birth years 1960 onward; older eligible cohorts also receive them. The pooled pretax account is assumed to belong to the primary person, with a surviving spouse treating it as their own after the modeled year of death. Each year's requirement uses the preceding modeled year-end pretax balance (the retirement starting balance in the first year) and the owner's whole-year age at the start of that modeled year. Spending withdrawals count toward the requirement. Payments are spread through the year and any remaining minimum is taken in a final partial lifetime year, before optional Roth conversions. After-tax proceeds not used for expenses remain in cash. RMDs are not converted to Roth. Calendar-year timing, first-year April deferral, separate spouse accounts, inherited nonspouse accounts, and the special table for a sole-beneficiary spouse more than ten years younger are not modeled.
  • For retirement before age 59½, the SEPP option enrolls the whole pretax balance in fixed monthly payments using 5% amortization and the IRS Single Life table. Extra withdrawals and Roth conversions from that account are blocked until the later of the fifth anniversary or age 59½; the owner's death ends the restriction. Other accounts must cover any gap, and an inaccessible pretax balance cannot prevent a spending shortfall. A final smaller payment on complete account depletion is allowed. The model maintains the series rather than modeling a broken series and its retroactive tax and interest. Actual eligibility, account separation, and an already-existing SEPP require separate verification.
  • Enter pension or annuity income in today's dollars. The annual increase applies from today, including the years before its payment start age. If you instead enter a future payment amount, this assumption can overstate that income.
  • The Social Security estimate uses the benefit you enter at age 67 and simplified claiming, spouse, and survivor calculations. Annual increases wait until the cumulative modeled price level exceeds the reference for the last benefit increase; a rebound following deflation does not raise benefits until that decline is recovered. This includes assumed deflation before retirement. General inflation is a proxy for CPI-W, and increases occur on retirement anniversaries rather than the official third-quarter comparison and December timing. See the SSA COLA formula. It is not an official benefit determination.
  • Income tax is charged as taxable income accumulates within each modeled year, using that year's brackets and deductions. Senior eligibility is fixed for the full modeled year from age at year-end, or age at death for a deceased person, rather than beginning at the birthday month. Modeled tax years start on retirement anniversaries, rather than calendar-year boundaries. Married households retain joint tax treatment and eligible deceased-spouse senior deductions through the modeled year of the first death, then use Single status. Living costs and benefits change in the month of death. Dependent-child eligibility for qualifying surviving spouse filing status is not modeled. The model does not reproduce withholding or estimated-tax payment dates.
  • Medicare surcharges use modeled income and the tax filing status from two years earlier when available. For the first two years, the planner estimates income from spending, benefits, required distributions, available pretax savings, and cash interest; it does not have your past tax returns. The initial estimate respects the cash reserve strategy and SEPP account restrictions. Cash principal and qualified Roth distributions do not count as ordinary income; nonqualified Roth earnings do. The highest tier starts at exactly $500,000 for Single or $750,000 for joint filing, and stays frozen through 2027. Starting in 2028, its separate August 2026 inflation base is approximated using the preceding modeled year's cumulative general price index. The individual threshold is rounded to the nearest $1,000; joint filers use 150% of it. Lower tiers retain their existing inflation projection from 2026. See Social Security Act section 1839(i)(5).
  • Assumption sensitivity compares up to 128 evenly spaced paths from the completed run with the same seeds. Each check separately removes general inflation, reduces base spending by 5% (keeping the plan’s property tax and home insurance amount), removes modeled federal income taxes and penalties, removes health premiums and care costs, uses constant investment returns at the entered annual means, or ends the household lifetime five years earlier. It reports the change in shortfall counts and recommends exploring the check with the largest positive reduction. These are hypothetical comparisons, not available tax exemptions or a causal decomposition; their effects overlap. No improvement means only that the check did not reduce shortfalls in this sample. Four-path sensitivity results remain previews.
  • Long-term care costs are included only when that option is enabled. The model sells the home at the start of the month when every surviving household member is in long-term care. It pays the remaining mortgage and places any positive net equity in cash, stopping mortgage payments and removing the property tax and home insurance entered under Housing from base spending. A spouse living outside care keeps the home unless financial accounts run out. Replacement rent applies only to people outside care. If the home is worth less than its mortgage, the remaining payoff comes from cash and portfolio withdrawals and can cause a shortfall. Mortgage principal follows a fixed-rate amortization schedule inferred from the entered balance, principal-and-interest payment, and remaining term, including payments before retirement. The payments must cover the balance over the entered term. A zero entered balance keeps the payment schedule without estimating debt at sale. Property tax and home insurance belong in annual base spending, with their yearly amount also entered under Housing (using a budget estimate fills it in), not as escrow in the mortgage payment. That amount is the same whether spending was typed or came from the budget. The sale does not include transaction costs or home-sale taxes. Other costs or events not entered or represented by the model can change the outcome.
  • Displayed balance ranges and ending balances describe simulated paths. They are not amounts you can expect or a promise that your portfolio will last.

Use of the results

Verify your inputs and compare more than one scenario. This tool does not provide individualized financial, investment, tax, legal, or insurance advice. Consult qualified professionals before making retirement, investment, tax, or insurance decisions.

Your scenario data

See the privacy notice for sign-in, billing, hosting, and data-removal details, or contact support.

The web planner saves scenarios in this browser's local storage and runs simulations in your browser. Report and backup files are created when you choose to export them. You are responsible for safeguarding exported files and making a backup before clearing browser data. The hosting service receives normal requests needed to deliver this page. If you sign in or subscribe, the Site checks your account's subscription status with Stripe. Stripe receives account and billing information but not your retirement scenarios or simulation inputs.

Model description reviewed September 2026. Review the assumptions again before relying on a later result.
